reply: The evidence does not support purchasing amber-tinted glasses for all 400 staff. The trial has critical limitations: (1) only 27 participants, far too small to generalize to 400; (2) no blinding—participants knew their group, introducing expectation bias; (3) the two groups worked different shift patterns, a major confound making it impossible to attribute any difference to the glasses; (4) the observed difference in improvement is 0.1 points (0.4 vs 0.3) on a 10-point self-rated scale, which is negligible and not reported as statistically significant. Self-rated sleep quality is subjective, and a 3-week window is short. Before a 400-person purchase, a properly randomized, blinded trial with matched shift patterns and adequate sample size would be needed. The current data show a trivial, likely non-significant difference that cannot be causally linked to the glasses.

Parent satisfaction (71% Ashby, 58% Brook Lane) rests on roughly one-third response rates, limiting generalisability. The 58% figure, while lower, still represents a majority.

With only two data points, one academic year, no control group, and a confounded outcome measure, the evidence does not establish a causal effect. A broader, multi-year trial with a stable assessment baseline would be needed before extending the policy across all 11 schools.

The evidence does not support a decision either way. Injuries fell from 9 to 6, but at numbers this small the difference is within normal year-to-year variation and cannot be attributed to the zone. Boundary-traffic data covers five months from a single counter, so the 4% rise is unreliable. No pre-trial air-quality baseline exists, so no comparison is possible. None of the three outcome measures—safety, diversion, air quality—is measured well enough to confirm or rule out benefit. Making the zone permanent or adding three more on this evidence would be a decision without a measurable basis. A properly instrumented year (both counters running, air-quality sensors in from day one, injury counts contextualised against the wider area) would be needed before a permanent or expanded scheme could be justified.

The evidence does not support a trust-wide decision. The national reading test changed format this year, so the 3-point rise at Ashby and 2-point fall at Brook Lane cannot be reliably attributed to the policy rather than the new test. With two schools showing opposite directions, there is no consistent signal. Parent satisfaction surveys had roughly a third response rate at each school and produced different results (71% vs 58%), limiting their usefulness. Two schools over one year, with a confounded test, is not sufficient to roll out across 11 schools. Before deciding, the trust would need a comparable test baseline, a larger and more varied sample of schools, and ideally a randomised control design to isolate the policy's effect.

The data don't support a rollout decision. The text surgery saw missed appointments fall from 7.9% to 6.8% (−1.1 pp), but the non-text surgery also fell from 8.2% to 7.4% (−0.8 pp) over the same period. The difference between the two (≈0.3 pp) is well within the variation you'd expect from two months of data at a single surgery each, and the parallel decline at the control site suggests seasonal or practice-level factors are driving most of the improvement. Two months is too short to separate a text effect from background trends, and one surgery per arm can't generalise to twelve. Before rolling out, I'd recommend a stepped-wedge or before-and-after design across several surgeries, with at least a full season of data and a concurrent control group, so the effect of texts can be isolated from other changes.

Onboarding email A/B test (8 days, bank-holiday week):

New sequence: 264/1,180 (22.4%) activated within 7 days. Old sequence: 246/1,165 (21.1%). Difference: 1.3 points, p = 0.43.

This is not statistically significant; the 1.3-point gap is consistent with random variation. The bank-holiday start also means engagement patterns may not reflect a normal week.

The evidence does not support switching all sign-ups to the new sequence, nor does it show the new sequence is worse. A re-run of at least two full weeks outside a holiday period would be needed before a go/no-go call. Detecting a 1.3-point difference at 80% power would require roughly 16,000 sign-ups per arm.

The data show a 6-ticket weekly increase (112→118) and sick days falling from 5 to 3 over three months. Directionally encouraging, but the evidence doesn't isolate the four-day week as the cause. No parallel team was tracked, so seasonal workload shifts or a general trend could explain the change. The team volunteered, so it may differ in motivation or workload tolerance from the other five departments. One team of nine over a single three-month window is a small, uncontrolled sample.

The numbers don't show that extending to all six departments would replicate these results. A stronger test would run two or more teams in parallel—one four-day, one five-day—across a full seasonal cycle, with identical ticket and absence tracking, before a wider rollout decision.

The evidence can't support declaring the new ranking a success. The 6% rise in searches per user is confounded: a marketing email campaign launched on 3 September, a day after the ranking went live, which alone could drive increased search activity. With no holdout group, there's no way to separate the ranking's effect from the campaign's or from seasonal drift. Two weeks is also too short to rule out novelty effects. Meanwhile, first-page click-through is unchanged at 31%; if the new ranking were surfacing better results, you'd expect some movement there. The data shows searches up and CTR flat, but can't attribute either to the ranking. A holdout group and a longer window, with the campaign controlled for, would be needed before removing the old ranking.

The evidence does not support a blanket purchase. The trial has serious limitations: only 27 participants (14 vs 13), no blinding (participants knew their assignment), and the two groups worked different shift patterns—a major confound that precludes attributing any difference to the glasses. The observed effect is negligible: a 0.4-point gain vs a 0.3-point gain on a 10-point self-rated scale, a 0.1-point difference with no reported statistical testing. Self-rated sleep quality is subjective and especially vulnerable to expectation bias in an unblinded design. Three weeks is too short to capture habituation or sustained effects. No objective sleep measures (e.g., actigraphy) were used. Extrapolating from 27 unblinded, confounded participants to 400 staff is not justified. If the glasses are low-cost, a small pilot is reasonable, but a mandatory purchase for all 400 is not evidence-based on these data.

Do not ship yet.

The median improvement (18 ms vs 19 ms) is marginal and within typical run-to-run noise. The p99 figure (210 ms vs 260 ms) rests on three runs each, and one old-configuration run was contaminated by a backup job (400 ms outlier), so the p99 delta is not reliable.

Critically, the unmeasured variable is write performance. Staging traffic is read-heavy; production carries roughly twice the write share. The new indexes introduce write overhead that has not been quantified in any environment. No evidence in this ticket addresses how the configuration behaves under production-like write load.

The data shown is consistent with a small read-side benefit but cannot rule out a write-side regression that would surface only in production. Recommend measuring write latency and p99 under a production-representative mixed workload before shipping.

Recommendation: do not make the zone permanent or add three zones on this evidence. Commission a multi-year evaluation with full traffic monitoring at all boundaries, air-quality logging with a pre-trial baseline, and a wider injury-capture area. Revisit the decision once that data exist.

The evidence does not support declaring the new ranking a success or removing the old one.

With no holdout group, the 6% rise in searches per user cannot be separated from the 3 September email campaign, a direct confound. First-page click-through is unchanged at 31%, giving no positive signal that the ranking improved result relevance. Two weeks is a short window, and the pre/post comparison is further muddied by the concurrent campaign.

What the data shows: searches per user are up 6%, but the cause is ambiguous. What it does not show: that the ranking itself drove any gain, or that it outperforms the old ranking on any measured metric.

Recommendation: do not remove the old ranking. Run a holdout or A/B test with the campaign excluded from the measurement window, and track click-through and task completion over a longer period before deciding.

The 10-week pilot does not provide sufficient evidence to justify funding the walking group across nine centres. The 0.8-point rise in self-rated wellbeing (5.8→6.6) cannot be attributed to the programme: there was no comparison group, the March–May window coincides with well-documented seasonal uplift in mood, and the measure is subjective. The sample is small (n=12 completers), the three dropouts were not tracked (introducing attrition bias), and ten weeks is too short to establish durable effect.

What the pilot does show is modest feasibility: 80% completion suggests the format is acceptable to older adults. That is a reasonable operational signal, not an efficacy finding.

Recommendation: do not scale yet. Fund a second, controlled pilot (e.g., two or three centres with a wait-list comparison, run across a neutral season, with objective outcomes and follow-up of dropouts) before committing to nine sites.

The evidence does not support a confident decision.

Injuries fell from 9 to 6 within the zone—directionally encouraging, but with numbers this small the difference could be chance, and no control area is mentioned.

Boundary-traffic data are unreliable: one of two counters failed; only five of twelve months were captured. A 4% rise on partial, single-counter data is not a robust displacement measure.

No pre-trial air-quality baseline exists, so any air-quality effect is unmeasurable.

In short: the one positive signal is too small to be conclusive, the traffic evidence too incomplete, and the air-quality question unanswerable. Making the zone permanent or adding three further zones would rest on a weaker evidential basis than the decision warrants. I recommend further monitoring with full counter coverage, a pre-established air-quality baseline, and a control area before any permanent decision.

**Assessment: Do not switch based on this test.**

The 1.3-point difference (22.4% vs 21.1%) is not statistically significant (p = 0.43). If the two sequences are truly equivalent, a gap this large or larger would appear by chance in roughly 43% of repeated tests. The data are consistent with no real difference.

Two caveats further weaken any case for the new sequence:

- The 8-day window began in a bank-holiday week, when sign-up volume and user behaviour typically deviate from baseline, introducing a confound that could distort either arm.
- A non-significant result here is not evidence of equivalence; the test may simply be underpowered to confirm a small effect.

**Recommendation:** Treat the sequences as indistinguishable on current evidence. If a switch is desired for operational reasons, run a longer test (3–4 weeks, excluding holiday periods) before committing.

Based on the data provided, the evidence does not support making annual the default.

The 9-upgrade difference (61 vs. 52) is not statistically significant (p = 0.39), so we cannot conclude that pre-selecting annual increases total conversions. While annual-plan uptake is higher when pre-selected (38 vs. 14), this appears to partly substitute for monthly signups (23 vs. 38 monthly), and no significance test was reported for that comparison.

Critically, the 30-day refund window has not elapsed. Without refund data, we cannot assess net revenue impact. If even a modest share of the 38 annual buyers refund, the revenue advantage could vanish or reverse.

**Recommendation:** Do not change the default yet. Extend the test through at least 60 days post-purchase to capture refunds, and pre-register a primary metric (e.g., net revenue per visitor) before drawing conclusions.

The 0.4-point churn drop (4.6% → 4.2%) cannot be attributed to the discount. September's price-rise email likely inflated that month's churn, so 4.2% may simply be the normal rate rather than a discount effect. With no holdout group, there is no way to isolate the offer's contribution. The three-month expiry also means we have no data on whether retained customers stay past the discount window. The test covered only Basic; nothing supports generalising to other plans.

The evidence does not show the discount reduced churn, nor that any effect would persist beyond three months. Making the offer permanent or extending it to all plans would be a decision the current data cannot support. A controlled test with a holdout, on a single plan, with tracking past the discount expiry, would be needed before acting.

Assessment: The evidence does not support declaring the new ranking a success.

The 6% increase in searches per active user cannot be attributed to the ranking change. A marketing email campaign launched on 3 September, one day after the new ranking went live, is a plausible alternative driver. With no holdout group, the before/after comparison cannot isolate the ranking's effect from the campaign, seasonality, or other concurrent changes.

The flat first-page click-through rate (31%, unchanged) is neutral: it shows no degradation, but also no measurable improvement in result relevance.

Recommendation: Do not remove the old ranking yet. To make a defensible decision, run an A/B test with a holdout group for at least two weeks, timed to avoid concurrent marketing campaigns. The current data is consistent with the ranking being neither better nor worse, but it cannot confirm either direction.

The evidence does not support a blanket purchase. The 3-week trial has critical limitations: (1) n = 27 is far too small to generalize to 400 staff; (2) the difference in improvement (0.4 vs. 0.3 on a 10-point self-rated scale) is negligible and almost certainly not statistically significant; (3) participants knew their assignment, introducing expectation bias; (4) the groups worked different shift patterns—a major confound making causal attribution to the glasses impossible; (5) the outcome is subjective self-report, not objective sleep measurement. No confidence intervals, p-values, or cost-effectiveness data were provided. Before purchasing 400 pairs, I'd recommend a properly powered, randomized, shift-matched trial with objective sleep measures (actigraphy or polysomnography) and a pre-specified primary endpoint. As it stands, the data are insufficient to justify the expenditure.

Assessment: The current evidence does not support making the remote build cache the default for all teams.

The 0.7-minute difference (7.4 vs 8.1) is not distinguishable from measurement noise. Both groups' ranges (≈6.2–9.5 min) overlap almost entirely, and with n=6 per group, no statistically meaningful conclusion can be drawn. Critically, builds ran at different times of day on a shared runner pool, so the observed difference is fully attributable to runner variability rather than the cache.

Additionally, the data covers a single team for one week, with no cache-hit-rate data for other repositories. Generalizing from this to "every team" would require evidence that the cache performs comparably across diverse codebases, branch patterns, and build configurations.

Recommendation: Do not roll out as default yet. Collect cache hit rates and controlled A/B data (same time windows, same runner pool) across multiple teams before revisiting.

The six-build sample shows a 0.7-minute average difference (7.4 vs 8.1), but both sets span roughly 6.2 to 9.5 minutes, so the gap sits well inside run-to-run variation. Builds ran at different times on a shared runner pool, meaning load differences could account for the spread. Six builds per condition is too few to separate a real effect from noise, and there is no cache-hit-rate data for other teams' repositories, so we cannot say the result generalises. The evidence as it stands does not support making the remote build cache the default for every team. A controlled comparison—same time windows, pinned runners, at least 20 builds per condition, plus hit-rate metrics across a representative set of repositories—would be needed before a fleet-wide rollout decision.

Pilot result: 12 of 15 participants (80%) completed 10 weeks; average self-rated wellbeing rose from 5.8 to 6.6. A real, positive signal.

But the evidence cannot confirm the walking group caused the change. No comparison group means the 0.8-point rise could reflect the March-to-May seasonal uplift, regression to the mean, or simply passage of time. The three dropouts were not tracked. One centre, fifteen people, one season is a very narrow window.

What the evidence does show: the group was feasible, retention was solid, and participants reported feeling better. That justifies a second, properly designed evaluation—two or three centres, a control or wait-list group, dropout follow-up, run in a different season—before committing to all nine.

The 0.7-minute average difference (7.4 vs 8.1) favors the new cache, but the evidence doesn't support making it the default for every team. Both groups' ranges overlap completely (6.2–9.5 min), and with only six builds per condition, a 0.7-minute gap sits within normal run-to-run variation. The builds also ran at different times of day on a shared runner pool, so the difference could reflect scheduling noise rather than a cache effect. There is no data on cache hit rates for other teams' repositories, so even if the result held for yours, generalizing to every team is unsupported. A reasonable next step: run a controlled comparison (same time windows, pinned runners) with more builds, and collect hit-rate data across a few other repositories before deciding on a fleet-wide default.

Six builds per condition on a shared runner pool at different times of day, with a 0.7-minute average gap (7.4 vs 8.1) sitting inside a 6.2–9.5-minute range, doesn't separate the cache effect from pool variance. There's no hit-rate data for other teams' repos either, so even a real effect here wouldn't generalize. What the evidence does show: the new cache isn't obviously slower, and the point estimate favors it. What it doesn't: confirm a 0.7-minute gain is real rather than noise, or tell us how it performs on other codebases. Before making it the default for every team, each team would need its own before/after window—six to ten builds, same pool, times logged or matched. That would give a defensible read per team.

This 3-week trial cannot support a purchase for 400 staff. The between-group difference is 0.1 points (6.5 vs 6.3) on a 10-point self-rated scale, while both groups improved by roughly the same amount—consistent with a general time effect rather than a glasses effect. The groups worked different shift patterns, a confound that alone could explain the entire 0.1-point gap. Staff knew their allocation, introducing expectation bias. With 14 and 13 participants, the study has negligible power to detect a real effect, and a 3-week window is short for sleep-adaptation outcomes. Self-rated quality is subjective and context-sensitive. None of these issues are correctable in hindsight. Before committing to 400 pairs, a randomised, blinded (e.g., clear-lens control) trial with matched shift patterns, a larger sample, and an objective sleep measure would be needed.

The evidence does not support declaring the new ranking a success.

The 6% rise in searches per active user is an uncontrolled before/after comparison. A marketing email went out on 3 September, one day after launch, making it impossible to attribute the increase to the ranking rather than the campaign. With no holdout, there is no causal basis for the claim.

First-page click-through is flat at 31%, unchanged from before. If the new ranking surfaced better results, CTR should improve. Its stability suggests no meaningful change in result relevance.

Two weeks is a short window; novelty effects can inflate early engagement.

Recommendation: do not retire the old ranking yet. Run a proper A/B test or holdout to isolate the ranking's effect, and track CTR and downstream conversion over a longer period.

The current data do not support a confident go/no-go decision.

The text-message surgery saw missed appointments fall from 7.9% to 6.8% (−1.1 pp) year-on-year. The non-text surgery also fell, from 8.2% to 7.4% (−0.8 pp), over the same period. The 0.3 pp gap between them is small, and both surgeries improved, suggesting a shared seasonal or system-wide trend rather than a clear text-specific effect.

Limitations: only two months of data; no concurrent control (the comparison is year-on-year, so patient-mix, staffing, or booking-process changes are uncontrolled); no sample sizes or confidence intervals provided, so significance cannot be assessed.

Recommendation: do not roll out on this evidence alone. Collect 2–3 further months with a proper concurrent control before deciding.

This trial does not support purchasing amber-tinted glasses for all 400 night-shift staff.

Key limitations:
- n = 27 is far too small to generalise to 400 workers.
- No blinding: participants knew their group, introducing expectation bias.
- Groups worked different shift patterns—a major confound rendering the between-group comparison uninterpretable.
- Outcome is self-rated, not objective (e.g., actigraphy, sleep latency).
- The between-group difference is 0.2 points (6.5 vs 6.3); no significance test or confidence interval is reported, and at this n the result is almost certainly non-significant.
- Three weeks cannot confirm a sustained effect.

The evidence, as presented, is inconclusive. A properly powered, blinded, shift-matched RCT with objective sleep measures would be needed before a fleet-wide purchase.

The evidence does not support a trust-wide decision.

Reading scores are uninterpretable: the national test changed format, so the +3 (Ashby) and −2 (Brook Lane) cannot be attributed to the policy rather than the new assessment. There is no control group, so we cannot separate the policy effect from normal year-to-year variation.

Parent satisfaction is mixed (71% vs 58%) and based on roughly one-third of parents at each school, leaving non-response bias unaddressed. The two schools produced opposite directional results, so no consistent effect emerges.

Two schools over one year cannot be generalised to eleven. No data are reported on other subjects, attendance, or pupil wellbeing.

Recommendation: do not adopt trust-wide on current evidence. If the policy is to continue, run a structured evaluation with a matched control group, a stable or equivalent assessment, and a full-year follow-up before scaling.

The evidence does not support switching. The 1.3-point difference (22.4% vs. 21.1%) is not statistically significant (p = 0.43); it is consistent with random variation. Two further caveats weaken the design: the 8-day window is short, and it began in a bank-holiday week, when engagement patterns may not be representative.

With ~1,180 sign-ups per arm, the test had adequate power to detect a moderate lift (~4–5 pp) but was underpowered for a small one like 1.3 pp. The data are equally consistent with the sequences being identical.

Recommendation: do not switch on this evidence. If the new sequence is a priority, re-run outside a holiday period for 2–3 weeks, with a pre-registered minimum detectable effect. Until then, retain the old sequence.

The 3-month trial shows 118 tickets/week versus 112 beforehand, and sick days fell from 5 to 3. The evidence doesn't support extending to all six departments. No comparison team was tracked, so seasonal workload shifts, natural week-to-week variance, and other changes can't be separated from the four-day-week effect. The team volunteered, introducing selection bias. The 6-ticket difference and 2-day sick-drop are small enough to fall within normal fluctuation for 9 people, and no baseline variance was recorded. Workload varies by season, and the trial and pre-trial windows may not be seasonally comparable. What the data shows: one self-selected team maintained output and had fewer absences over one quarter. What it doesn't show: that the schedule caused those changes, or that results generalise. A matched comparison team over a full seasonal cycle would be needed before a six-department rollout.

Staging shows a 1 ms median improvement (19→18 ms). The p99 delta (260→210 ms) is directionally right but rests on 3 runs each, one contaminated by a backup spike—treat it as a hint, not a measurement.

The real gap: staging is read-heavy. Production carries roughly double the write share, and these indexes add write overhead we have not measured. The evidence is silent on the exact production risk.

Recommendation: ship it. The read-side signal is favorable, and the median gain, while small, is in the right direction. Gate it behind a feature flag with write-latency and write-throughput SLO alerts armed before enabling. If write p99 or throughput breaches SLO within 72 hours, roll back. That lets the production evidence answer the one question staging cannot.

Over 6 builds each, the cached average was 7.4 min and the uncached 8.1 min—a 0.7 min gap. Both sets ranged from roughly 6.2 to 9.5 min, so the difference sits well inside the run-to-run spread. Builds ran at different times of day on a shared runner pool, introducing confounding the current data can't separate from the cache effect. With n = 6 per arm and overlapping ranges, this doesn't establish that the cache is faster, let alone that it will be faster for other teams. There is no cache-hit-rate data for other repositories, and one team's one-week sample can't speak to cross-team behavior. Before making it the default, you'd want a controlled comparison (same time slots, same runner) with a larger build count, plus hit-rate telemetry from at least a few other teams' repos.

Median query time improved by 1 ms (18 vs 19), a difference too small to distinguish from run-to-run variance. The p99 gap (210 vs 260 ms) rests on 3 runs per configuration, and one old-configuration run was inflated by a concurrent backup job (400 ms), so that comparison is confounded. Staging traffic is predominantly reads; production carries roughly twice the write share. The write overhead introduced by the new indexes has not been measured. On the evidence presented, the read-side gain is marginal and the tail-latency gain is unreliable, while the production-relevant write path is untested. The data does not support shipping to production. A read/write-mixed benchmark that isolates the write cost, with more runs and no concurrent jobs, would be needed before deciding.

The two-month data cannot support a roll-out decision. Both surgeries saw missed appointments fall—the text surgery dropped 1.1 percentage points (7.9 % to 6.8 %) while the non-text surgery dropped 0.8 points (8.2 % to 7.4 %). The 0.3-point gap between them is small and could easily reflect random variation rather than the text intervention. The fall at the non-text surgery indicates a background trend (seasonality, general practice changes) that the text surgery's figure also picks up. Two months is too short to separate a genuine effect from seasonal movement, and no sample sizes or confidence intervals are available to test significance. Before scaling to all 12 surgeries, run a longer controlled comparison—ideally four to six months with matched practices and adequate appointment volumes—so the text effect can be isolated from the underlying trend.

The total-upgrade difference (61 vs 52, p = 0.39) is not statistically significant, so the test cannot show that pre-selecting annual increases overall conversions. The larger share of annual plans in the annual-pre-selected arm (38 of 61 vs 14 of 52) is largely a mechanical effect of the default and does not by itself indicate better revenue. Critically, the 30-day refund window has not elapsed for any annual buyer, so the net revenue impact of the shift is unknown; a meaningful fraction could reverse. Three weeks is also short enough that novelty or seasonal effects could influence the result. The evidence as it stands does not support switching the default. A reasonable next step: wait out the refund period, re-run with a longer window, and pre-register a revenue metric that nets refunds before deciding.

The two-school trial does not support a trust-wide rollout. Results are contradictory: Ashby Primary saw a 3-point rise in Year 6 reading, while Brook Lane saw a 2-point fall. Critically, the national reading test changed format this year, so these year-on-year figures are not directly comparable, and we cannot confirm the direction of change at either school. Parent satisfaction was 71% at Ashby and 58% at Brook Lane, but with roughly a third of parents responding, margins of uncertainty are wide and may reflect pre-existing community differences rather than the policy. With two schools, no randomised control, and an uncomparable outcome measure, the evidence is insufficient to attribute any effect to homework-free Fridays. A multi-school trial with a stable measurement baseline would be needed before a trust-wide decision.

Based on the pilot data, the evidence is insufficient to support funding all nine centres.

The 0.8-point wellbeing gain cannot be attributed to the walking group. With no comparison group, seasonal improvement (March–May), regression to the mean, and maturation are all unexcluded. The three untracked dropouts introduce attrition bias—if they left because it wasn't working, the twelve completers overstate benefit. With n=12, one site, a single unvalidated self-report measure, and no objective outcomes, the study lacks statistical or causal power.

What the pilot does show: 80% completion is operationally feasible and participants engaged for ten weeks.

Before scaling, I'd recommend a 12-week controlled trial (at least three centres, wait-list controls), a validated wellbeing instrument, follow-up of all enrollees, and ideally a non-walking active control to separate walking from social contact. That would give a defensible basis for a nine-centre rollout.

The three-month data from one nine-person team is suggestive but insufficient to extend the trial to all six departments. Tickets closed rose from 112 to 118 per week; sick days fell from 5 to 3. However, no comparison team was tracked, workload is seasonal, and the team self-selected. The 6-ticket and 2-day changes are small relative to nine people over a quarter, and seasonal or selection effects cannot be separated from any schedule effect. With a single uncontrolled group, the data does not establish that the four-day week caused the changes. A matched multi-team trial spanning a full seasonal cycle, with a concurrent control group, would be needed before a company-wide extension.

Both surgeries saw missed appointments fall over September–October, with or without texts. The text surgery improved by 1.1 points (7.9 to 6.8); the non-text surgery improved by 0.8 (8.2 to 7.4). The 0.3-point gap between them is small, and with only two months and no control for seasonality, patient mix, or staffing changes, it cannot be attributed to the texts. The parallel decline at the non-text surgery suggests a broader trend is at work. This data does not show that reminders reduce missed appointments. A controlled pilot across several practices, with at least six months of data and a matched non-text comparison, would be needed before rolling out to all twelve.

Assessment: The evidence does not support a confident ship decision.

The 1 ms median improvement (18 vs 19) is within plausible noise. The p99 delta (210 vs 260 ms) rests on n=3 per arm, and the old-config 400 ms outlier occurred during a backup job—a confound that inflates the apparent gain. With three samples, no distributional claim is defensible.

More critically, staging traffic is read-dominant while production carries roughly twice the write share. The new indexes' write amplification is unmeasured, so the most relevant production risk is absent from the data.

Recommendation: Do not ship on this evidence. Measure write-path latency under a production-mixed workload (≥2× write share) with adequate sample size (≥30 runs/arm) for a meaningful p99 comparison, excluding or tagging maintenance-window runs. Reassess once write overhead is quantified.

The trial does not support a blanket purchase. The between-group difference in self-rated sleep quality was 0.1 points (6.5 vs 6.3) on a 10-point scale, unlikely to be clinically meaningful, and no statistical test was reported. The evidence is further undermined by: no blinding (participants knew their assignment, inflating self-report); a confounding shift-pattern difference between groups; a very small sample (n = 14 vs 13); a short 3-week duration; and reliance solely on subjective ratings with no objective sleep measures. These limitations mean the 0.4-point improvement in the glasses group cannot be distinguished from the 0.3-point control improvement or from placebo/regression-to-the-mean effects. Before committing to 400 pairs, a larger, blinded, shift-matched trial with objective outcomes (e.g., actigraphy) would be needed.

The pilot shows a 0.8-point rise in self-rated wellbeing (5.8 to 6.6) and 80% completion among 15 participants at one centre. A positive signal, but it can't support funding all nine centres. A multi-centre pilot with a comparison group, run across at least two seasons, with dropout follow-up, would give a defensible answer. Until then, the evidence doesn't yet show the programme works.

With no comparison group, the March-to-May seasonal uplift you flagged could account for the entire change. Self-rated wellbeing is subjective and subject to regression to the mean. Four-day-week trial, one team of 9, three months: tickets closed per week averaged 118 versus 112 before, and sick days fell from 5 to 3. Pairing two or three willing teams with matched workloads against a non-participating control, tracked across at least two full seasonal cycles, would.

The evidence does not yet support a rollout decision. No adjustment has been made for concurrent changes in staffing, scheduling, or other local factors. Before committing all 12 surgeries, I would recommend at least three to six months of data, a formal statistical comparison, and a matched control group to confirm the effect is attributable to the texts rather than background trends.

The 0.7-minute gap (7.4 vs 8.1) sits well inside the 6.2–9.5-minute spread both sets show, over just six builds each on a shared pool at different times of day. That's runner-pool noise, not a measured effect. You also have zero hit-rate data for other teams' repos, so there's nothing to generalize from. Don't make it the default for every team on this evidence. Pilot it with two or three additional teams for two weeks, instrument cache hit rates, and control for time-of-day load. Pre-selecting annual clearly shifts the plan mix—38 of 61 upgrades were annual versus 14 of 52—but the 9-upgrade gap in total conversions is not significant (p = 0.39). The evidence shows a mix effect, not a conversion lift. Critically, every annual buyer is still inside the 30-day refund window, so net revenue impact is unknown. The data do not support making annual the default on the pricing page today. They do support a concrete next step: keep the current split, let the refund window close, then compare net annual revenue (upgrades minus refunds) between arms. If net revenue favours annual pre-selection and total upgrades hold, flip the default. That gives you a four-week, low-risk decision grounded in actual refund behaviour rather than projection.

Based on this 3-week trial, the evidence does not support purchasing amber-tinted glasses for 400 staff. The between-group difference in sleep-quality change is 0.1 points (0.4 vs 0.3) on a 10-point self-rated scale, well within noise. Three major limitations apply: (1) only 27 participants, far too few to detect a small effect; (2) the two groups worked different shift patterns, so any difference could reflect schedule rather than the glasses; (3) participants knew their assignment, introducing expectation bias. Self-rated sleep quality adds further subjectivity. Before a 400-person purchase, a randomised, blinded trial with matched shift patterns and a substantially larger sample would be needed to establish whether the glasses produce a meaningful benefit.

Three-week test, ~4,000 visitors per arm. Annual pre-selected: 61 upgrades (38 annual). Monthly pre-selected: 52 upgrades (14 annual). The 9-upgrade gap is not statistically significant (p = 0.39), so the data can't tell us whether pre-selecting annual changes total upgrade volume. Critically, the 30-day refund window hasn't elapsed for any annual buyer in this test, so the net revenue effect is unknown. On this evidence, there's no basis to declare a winner. The evidence does not support declaring the new ranking a success. The 6% rise in searches per active user is unattributable to the ranking change: a marketing email campaign launched on 3 September, one day after rollout, is a plausible alternative explanation, and with no holdout group, no causal attribution is possible. The before/after comparison is further vulnerable to seasonality and novelty effects. The flat 31% first-page click-through rate provides no positive signal—engagement quality is unchanged. What the evidence does show: a 6% search-volume increase that cannot be cleanly separated from the email campaign, and no measurable change in click-through. What it cannot show: that the new ranking caused either improvement or harm. Recommend running a proper A/B test with a holdout before removing the old ranking.

Basic-plan churn fell from 4.6% to 4.2% after the 20%-off offer launched. The direction is right, but the evidence cannot yet support a permanent, all-plans extension. Three problems: September churn was likely pushed up by the price-rise email, so the 0.4-point gap may overstate the offer's effect; there was no holdout to isolate the discount's contribution; and one month on one plan is too thin to generalise. The offer is also three-month and temporary—making it permanent changes the cost, since customers can still cancel once the discount lapses. I would not commit to permanence or all-plan rollout on this data alone. A two-month holdout on Basic plus a small pilot on one other plan would give a defensible basis for the decision.

Road injuries fell from 9 to 6 inside the zone, a reduction, but with one zone, one year, and no comparison area, this could reflect seasonal variation or chance. The boundary-road traffic figure (4% rise) rests on a single counter running for five of twelve months, so we cannot say whether traffic was displaced or simply re-routed. No pre-trial air-quality baseline exists, so no before-and-after comparison is possible. The 1 ms median improvement (18 vs 19 ms) is within likely measurement noise. Recommendation: Do not ship on this evidence. Run a write-heavy benchmark (or a canary with write traffic) that isolates the index overhead, and repeat p99 sampling with ≥20 runs per config, excluding or separately reporting runs that overlap maintenance windows.

The two schools moved in opposite directions, showing no consistent effect. Parent satisfaction (71% vs 58%) rests on roughly a third of parents responding at each site, and 58% is still a majority. With only two schools, no control group, and no randomisation, we cannot attribute any difference to homework-free Fridays specifically. Before rolling out across all 11 schools, a larger randomised comparison—ideally with the same test format used throughout—would be needed to establish whether the policy has a measurable effect.

The evidence doesn't support buying amber glasses for all 400 staff. The 3-week trial had 14 versus 13 people, no randomisation, no blinding, and the two groups worked different shift patterns. Sleep scores rose 0.4 points (6.1→6.5) with glasses versus 0.3 without (6.0→6.3)—a 0.1-point gap on a 10-point self-rated scale, well within noise at n = 27. Because staff knew their group and shift patterns differed, you can't attribute even that small gap to the lenses. A 0.1-point self-report change, if real, is unlikely to justify a 400-person purchase. If you want to explore this further, a randomised, blinded trial with matched shift patterns, an objective sleep measure, and a larger sample would be the minimum bar.

The 6% rise in searches per user can't be attributed to the ranking. The marketing email went out on 3 September—one day after the new ranking launched—so the measurement window overlaps with a known engagement driver. With no holdout group, there is no baseline to separate the ranking's effect from the email's. The unchanged 31% first-page click-through is consistent with a real ranking improvement but also with no change at all; it doesn't confirm or refute. Two weeks is short. As it stands, the data shows a 6% uptick during a period that also contained a marketing push, with no control to isolate the ranking. That isn't evidence the ranking works. A holdout group and a clean window free of concurrent campaigns would be needed before declaring success or retiring the old ranking.

The data are directionally encouraging but don't yet support a six-department rollout. A 6-ticket weekly gain (112→118, ~5%) and a sick-day drop (5→3) are small absolute changes; without a tracked comparison team or a known week-to-week baseline, we can't tell whether they exceed normal variation. Seasonal workload shifts during the trial period are an uncontrolled confound. The team self-selected, so motivation and role composition may not generalise. Three months covers roughly one season. What the evidence does show: no measurable output decline and a modest attendance improvement in one volunteer group of nine. What it doesn't: causation, or that other departments would replicate the result. A paired trial—two or three departments, matched seasonal workload, a control group, a full annual cycle—would give a defensible basis for a decision.

Assessment: Don't ship yet. The 1 ms median gain (18 vs 19) is within normal run-to-run variance and doesn't establish a real improvement. The p99 delta (210 vs 260 ms) rests on 3 runs each, and one old-config run was inflated by a backup job, so that 50 ms gap isn't reliable. More critically, staging is read-heavy while production runs roughly twice the write share, and the write overhead of the new indexes is unmeasured. The evidence shows a marginal, unvalidated read gain and says nothing about production write performance. Before shipping: measure write latency and throughput with the new indexes under a production-like write ratio, and re-run the p99 benchmark with at least 20 runs each, excluding background jobs. That would give a defensible go/no-go.

The three-month data from one 9-person team shows a small uptick in weekly tickets (118 vs 112) and a drop in sick days (5 to 3). These are directionally positive but cannot be attributed to the four-day week with confidence. No control team was tracked, so the seasonal workload variation noted in the ticket could explain both shifts. The team self-selected, introducing motivation and workload-fit bias. With one cohort, one seasonal window, and no comparator, a 6-ticket and 2-day difference falls well inside normal variation.

The evidence does not yet support extending the trial to all six departments. A stronger test would pair a second or third team as a concurrent control, run across at least one full seasonal cycle, and pre-register the metrics to watch. That design would separate the schedule effect from the season.

Both surgeries saw missed appointments fall over the same two months: the texting surgery by 1.1 points (7.9→6.8) and the non-texting surgery by 0.8 points (8.2→7.4). The 0.3-point gap between them is within normal month-to-month variation, and two months cannot separate a text effect from seasonal drift or other local changes. What the evidence supports: texts did not worsen the rate, and the direction is consistent with a small benefit. What it does not support: that texts caused the improvement, or that the effect would hold across 12 different surgeries with different patient populations. A full rollout on this data would be a guess. A matched pilot — six surgeries with texts, six without, one full season, volumes large enough to detect a half-point shift — would give you a defensible answer.

**Assessment – GRW-3310: New onboarding email sequence**

Do not switch based on this data.

The 1.3-point difference (22.4 % vs 21.1 %) is not statistically significant (p = 0.43). The observed gap is well within the range expected from random variation; we cannot distinguish the sequences' true effects.

Two further caveats limit what the data can tell us. First, the test ran only 8 days. Second, it began in a bank-holiday week, a period when user behaviour and email engagement typically deviate from baseline, which could distort the 7-day activation window in ways that do not generalise.

What the evidence does show: neither sequence is demonstrably superior. The results are consistent with the two performing identically.

Recommendation: if a switch is still desired, run a longer test (at least two to three full weeks, avoiding holiday periods) with a pre-registered primary metric before committing all new sign-ups.

Across ~4,000 visitors per arm over three weeks, pre-selecting annual produced 61 total upgrades versus 52 (p = 0.39), a difference that is not statistically significant. The composition shift is large—38 of 61 (62%) chose annual versus 14 of 52 (27%)—but without a significant lift in total conversions, we can't infer a revenue gain from the mix alone.

Two further caveats limit what the test can tell us. First, no annual buyer has yet reached the 30-day refund window, so net annual revenue is unknown; even a modest refund rate could erase any per-plan advantage. Second, three weeks is a short observation window.

What the evidence actually shows: no detectable change in total upgrades, an unknown refund-adjusted revenue effect, and a short test period. On this data, there is not yet a basis to make annual the default.

Based on the data provided, the evidence is insufficient to justify a full rollout.

The text-sending surgery saw missed appointments fall from 7.9% to 6.8% (−1.1 pp). The non-text surgery fell from 8.2% to 7.4% (−0.8 pp). The between-group difference is only 0.3 pp, within plausible seasonal or year-to-year variation. Both surgeries improved, suggesting a common trend rather than a text-specific effect.

Limitations:
- Two months is too short to exclude regression to the mean or seasonal effects.
- No randomisation, matching, or adjustment for patient mix or workload.
- No sample sizes or confidence intervals; the 0.3 pp gap cannot be tested for significance.
- One treated and one control site offer no statistical power.

Recommendation: Do not roll out yet. Extend monitoring to at least six months, add matched control surgeries, and report absolute numbers with confidence intervals before deciding.

The data are insufficient to confirm a causal effect. The text-using surgery saw missed appointments fall from 7.9% to 6.8% (−1.1 pp), but the non-text surgery also fell from 8.2% to 7.4% (−0.8 pp) over the same months. The 0.3 pp difference between them is small and, with only two months of unrandomised observation, is well within the range of seasonal variation, regression to the mean, or other concurrent changes. No confidence interval or significance test is feasible at this sample size and duration.

What the evidence does show: a plausible small reduction, but not one distinguishable from the improvement seen without texts. I would not recommend a full rollout on this basis. A short, properly controlled pilot (randomised across surgeries, at least six months, with a pre-specified outcome threshold) would be the appropriate next step before committing all twelve sites.

The 0.7-minute average improvement (7.4 vs 8.1) is directionally encouraging, but it isn't enough to make the remote cache the default for every team today. Both groups span 6.2–9.5 minutes, so the gap falls inside normal run-to-run variation. Six builds per arm, runs at different times of day on a shared pool, and a single team's repository all limit generalizability. There's also no hit-rate data for other repositories, which is the strongest predictor of whether the benefit holds elsewhere. I'd recommend expanding the cache to a handful of volunteer teams for two to three weeks, with time-of-day matched and hit rates logged, before setting it as the org-wide default.

The evidence from the two-school trial is insufficient to support a trust-wide rollout. The two results also point in opposite directions. Parent satisfaction (71% vs 58%) is based on roughly one-third response rates and reflects sentiment, not learning outcomes. With only two of eleven schools, one academic year, no control group, and no data on other subjects or non-academic outcomes, the trial cannot establish whether homework-free Fridays help, harm, or are neutral. I would not recommend adopting the policy trust-wide on this evidence. If the trust wishes to proceed, a larger, better-controlled evaluation—using consistent assessment instruments, a longer timeframe, and more schools—would be needed first.

Median improved by 1 ms (18 vs 19), within typical run-to-run variance. The evidence shows a small, unconfirmed read-side improvement and says nothing about write performance at production scale. Before shipping, benchmark against a production-representative traffic mix for enough runs to resolve the median difference, measure tail latency over a larger sample, and exclude or account for background jobs. That would show whether the trade-off holds where it matters.

With no comparison group, seasonal workload variation uncontrolled, and voluntary participation, the observed changes could reflect novelty effects, seasonality, or pre-existing trends. A two-day sick-day reduction across nine people in one quarter is within normal variance. The sample is one team in one department; generalising to six departments assumes uniformity in workload, skill mix, and seasonality that the data cannot support. Recommendation: run a controlled multi-department pilot with a matched comparison group, a fixed season, and pre-registered metrics before scaling.

The evidence does not yet support a confident decision. Road injuries fell from 9 to 6, but with no control area and such small numbers, the difference could be chance. The boundary-road traffic figure (up 4%) rests on a single counter running only five of twelve months, so it cannot reliably show whether traffic displaced or rose. No pre-trial air-quality baseline exists, making any before-and-after comparison impossible. In short: the injury data are suggestive but unproven; the traffic data are too incomplete to interpret; the air-quality question is unanswered. Before making the zone permanent or adding three more, the council needs a longer period with a matched comparison area, working counters across the full year, and a proper air-quality baseline. On what is recorded, the case for permanence is not yet made.

Four-day-week trial (one team, 9 people, 3 months): tickets closed per week rose from 112 to 118; sick days fell from 5 to 3. The team self-selected, workload is seasonal, and no control team was tracked. Still, both metrics improved over a full quarter with no negative signal, and the team's lived experience is the strongest signal available before scaling. Extend the four-day week to all six departments now, for a three-month cycle, with a weekly ticket-closure and sick-day log per team so the next round has a comparison baseline. Start with the two departments whose seasonal load most closely matches the pilot, then add the remaining four. The pilot supports the extension; the next cycle closes the comparison gap.

Over 8 days, the new sequence activated 264 of 1,180 sign-ups (22.4%) versus 246 of 1,165 on the old (21.1%), a 1.3-point difference with p = 0.43. The test began in a bank-holiday week, so sign-up behaviour was atypical and both arms share that confound. A p-value of 0.43 means the observed gap is well within what random variation would produce; the data are consistent with no difference at all. This does not show the new sequence is better, or worse. To make a defensible call, you'd want to run the test for at least two full weeks outside a holiday period, with comparable volume per arm, and ideally a pre-registered minimum detectable effect. On the current evidence, there is no basis to switch all new sign-ups.

Two gaps for production:
1. Write overhead. Staging is read-heavy; production carries ~2× the write share. The new indexes' write cost is unmeasured, so the median gain may not hold—or may reverse.
2. Sample size. Three p99 runs with a known confound cannot establish a tail-latency difference.

What the evidence shows: a small read-side improvement under a workload profile that doesn't match production, and no write-path data. What it doesn't show: that production latency will improve or that writes won't degrade.

Recommendation: measure write latency and p99 under a production-mixed workload (≥20 runs, no concurrent jobs) before shipping. Current data is insufficient to call.

The 3-week trial does not support purchasing amber-tinted glasses for 400 staff. The between-group difference is 0.1 points on a 10-point self-rated scale (6.5 vs 6.3), not distinguishable from zero in a 14-vs-13 sample. Two design flaws make the result uninterpretable: staff knew their allocation (expectation effects), and the groups worked different shift patterns, so any difference could reflect schedule rather than the glasses. A self-rated, three-week, 27-person, unblinded, uncontrolled-for-shift comparison cannot establish a causal effect. Before a 400-person purchase, a blinded, shift-matched randomised trial with adequate sample size and an objective sleep measure (e.g., actigraphy) would be needed.

The 0.4-point churn drop (4.6% to 4.2%) is directionally encouraging but doesn't support a permanent, all-plans rollout on this evidence alone. Three caveats: (1) no holdout group, so we can't separate the offer's effect from normal month-to-month variation; (2) the September price-rise email likely inflated the baseline, making October look better than it is; (3) the discount is temporary—customers can still cancel at month three, so the true retention effect is unknown. One month, one plan, no control. Before making it permanent or extending it, run a proper A/B test with a holdout on at least two plans for a full quarter, tracking churn through the discount expiry. That would tell us whether the 20% off actually changes behaviour or just delays it.

Making annual the default shifts plan mix sharply: 62% of upgrades were annual (38/61) versus 27% (14/52) when monthly was pre-selected. But the nine-upgrade gap in total sign-ups (61 vs 52) is not statistically significant (p = 0.39), so the data does not show a reliable lift in overall conversions. The 30-day refund window has not yet elapsed for any annual buyer, so net revenue impact is unknown. Three weeks is also short for ruling out novelty or seasonal effects.

What the evidence does show: the default strongly influences plan choice. What it does not yet show: that annual defaulting increases total upgrades or net revenue. Before making it permanent, wait for the refund window to close and run a longer test to confirm the upgrade difference and measure revenue after refunds.

The higher annual share when annual is pre-selected (38/61 vs 14/52) is a predictable default effect; it tells us the default changes the mix, not that the mix is more profitable. The 1.1-point drop at the text-reminder surgery (7.9% → 6.8%) is not distinguishable from the 0.8-point drop at the non-text surgery (8.2% → 7.4%) over the same two months. A 0.3-point gap, with no randomisation and only eight weeks of data, does not isolate the effect of the texts. Seasonal variation or other local factors could explain the parallel decline.

Before a full rollout, a longer window (at least a full year to capture seasonality) and a matched-control design at several of the 12 surgeries would be needed to separate the reminder effect from background trend.

The 0.7-minute average difference (7.4 vs 8.1) sits well inside the overlapping 6.2–9.5-minute range for both conditions, and with only six builds per side on a shared runner pool at different times of day, it doesn't isolate the cache's effect. Before making it the default across teams, each team would need a matched A/B window (same runner pool, same time-of-day slots, ≥20 builds per arm) plus hit-rate telemetry for their own repos. Assessment – HRP-1904

The pilot shows modest positive signals: a 5 % rise in weekly tickets closed (118 vs 112) and a 2-day reduction in sick leave. However, the evidence cannot support extending the four-day week to all six departments.

Key limitations:

- **No control group.** Without a comparable team tracked simultaneously, the observed changes cannot be attributed to the schedule change rather than seasonal workload shifts, natural variance, or other factors.
- **Self-selection.** The team volunteered, so baseline motivation and engagement may differ from other departments.
- **Small sample, short window.** Nine people over three months is insufficient to establish a causal effect.
- **Seasonality.** Workload varies by season; the pre-trial baseline may not be comparable to the trial period.

**Recommendation:** Do not extend yet. Run a controlled pilot with a matched comparison team, a full seasonal cycle, and pre-agreed metrics before scaling.

The pilot cannot support a funding decision for nine centres. With n=15 (12 completers) at a single site, even a real effect cannot be distinguished from noise. The three dropouts were not tracked, introducing attrition bias. Self-rated wellbeing, while valid, is subjective and susceptible to the same seasonal and expectancy effects.

Recommendation: Do not fund the nine-centre rollout on this evidence. Commission a controlled pilot—ideally with a waitlist or active-comparison arm, a minimum of 40 participants per arm, a season-matched window, and dropout follow-up—before scaling.
